articles.headline: OFAC Designates Four Iranian 'Oil Trustees' for Sanctions Evasion
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced sanctions on four Iranian individuals, identifying them as 'oil trustees' who facilitate illicit oil sales to evade U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade. These individuals are accused of collecting proceeds from international oil sales, often retaining funds for personal gain, and supporting Tehran's efforts to circumvent restrictions.

Among those designated are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the Iranian Football Federation's president. Bavand is noted for his role in overseeing sanctioned oil sales and allocating crude to intermediaries with outstanding debts.

The sanctions also target Mohammadhossein Servati, involved in companies brokering Iranian oil shipments to Chinese 'teapot' refineries, and Mojtaba Arabnejad, who has purchased aircraft parts for the sanctioned Mahan Air and overseen oil sales supporting the airline. These designations freeze any assets under U.S. jurisdiction and generally prohibit transactions with them.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Cuba Frequently Asked Questions Amid Expanded Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has released new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning Cuba, coinciding with recent expansions of U.S. sanctions targeting the island nation. These FAQs aim to provide clarity and guidance to individuals and entities navigating the evolving regulatory landscape surrounding Cuba.

The issuance follows President Trump's Executive Order 14404 in May 2026, which broadened the scope of U.S. sanctions against Cuba, introducing new authorities to target key sectors of the Cuban economy and impose secondary sanctions on foreign financial institutions.

The expanded sanctions framework, which operates alongside the longstanding Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR), also includes prohibitions on U.S. banks maintaining accounts for Cuban entrepreneurs and restricts certain payments connected to Cuba from passing through the U.S. financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations, Issues New General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global criminal networks that pose threats to national security and financial stability.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued an Illicit Drugs General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. This license aims to mitigate unintended consequences of sanctions while maintaining pressure on illicit drug trafficking operations.

Furthermore, OFAC released an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the sanctions regime imposed in response to Russia's actions. These updates are crucial for entities engaged in transactions involving Russia to ensure compliance with evolving regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented new counter terrorism designations, targeting individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist organizations and activities globally. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt the financial networks that enable terrorism and protect the international financial system from abuse.

The designations aim to isolate these actors from the U.S. financial system and prevent them from accessing resources that could be used to fund their operations. This move reinforces the U.S. government's resolve to combat terrorism through comprehensive financial measures.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the implications of these actions, are available through OFAC's official channels. These designations underscore the dynamic nature of counter-terrorism finance and the continuous need for vigilance.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Authorities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under both counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. These actions target individuals and networks involved in illicit drug trafficking and those providing material support to terrorist organizations.

The dual nature of these designations highlights the interconnectedness of various illicit activities and the U.S. government's strategy to address these threats comprehensively. By targeting both narcotics and terrorism, OFAC aims to dismantle multifaceted criminal enterprises.

These designations result in the blocking of all property and interests in property of the designated persons that are within U.S. jurisdiction, and generally prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them.

articles.headline: OFAC Publishes Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has published an update regarding Iran designations. This update provides additional information or modifications to existing listings under the various sanctions programs targeting Iran.

Such updates are routine as OFAC continuously reviews and refines its sanctions lists to ensure accuracy and effectiveness. Entities and individuals involved in Iran-related transactions are advised to consult the latest guidance.

The specific details of this update, including any additions, removals, or modifications to existing entries, are available on the OFAC website, emphasizing the dynamic nature of sanctions compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities that support the Iranian regime's destabilizing actions. These designations are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran.

The actions aim to further disrupt networks that provide financial, material, technological, or other support to designated Iranian entities or individuals. This includes those involved in proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities, ballistic missile development, or support for terrorism.
These new designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to preventing Iran from acquiring resources that could be used to advance its illicit programs and regional malign activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Activities; Imposes Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced significant designations targeting entities involved in cyber-related malicious activities and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt sophisticated illicit networks that pose threats to U.S. national security and the global financial system.

Concurrently, OFAC also imposed new Cuba designations and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to increase pressure on the Cuban regime and its supporters, particularly those involved in human rights abuses or undermining democratic processes.

The cyber-related designations highlight the increasing focus on digital threats, while the transnational criminal organization designations target groups engaged in a wide range of illicit activities, from drug trafficking to money laundering. The Cuba actions further restrict financial interactions with designated Cuban entities.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Iran-related Designations and Updates Listings; Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and provided updates to certain existing Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the U.S. government's comprehensive strategy to counter Iran's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, providing guidance and warnings to the public and financial institutions regarding potential sanctions evasion schemes. This alert aims to enhance awareness and compliance within the financial sector.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions. These adjustments reflect the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy and aim to provide clarity for humanitarian aid and other authorized transactions in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, providing updated guidance to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions.

General Licenses are crucial tools that allow for specific activities to proceed that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. The amendment reflects ongoing policy adjustments and aims to facilitate legitimate trade and humanitarian efforts while maintaining sanctions pressure.

Entities and individuals engaging in Iran-related activities are advised to review the amended General License carefully to understand any changes to permitted transactions and reporting requirements.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting North Korea, aiming to disrupt the regime's ability to fund its weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs. These actions are part of a concerted international effort to enforce United Nations Security Council resolutions.

The designations target individuals and entities involved in activities such as illicit financial facilitation, procurement of prohibited goods, and generation of revenue for the North Korean regime. This includes efforts to counter North Korean IT worker schemes.
These measures underscore the U.S. commitment to preventing North Korea from advancing its illicit weapons programs and to promoting denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to address ongoing instability, human rights abuses, and corruption within the region.
The designations target individuals and entities whose activities contribute to the conflict and exploitation of resources in the DRC. This includes efforts to counter Sudanese military commanders.
These measures are intended to promote peace, stability, and respect for human rights in the DRC by disrupting the financial networks of those perpetuating violence and illicit activities.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Agrees to Pay $1,529,685 for OFAC Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to remit $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs.
The settlement addresses alleged breaches of U.S. sanctions regulations, highlighting the importance of robust compliance programs for companies operating internationally.

Details of the specific violations leading to this penalty are outlined in the enforcement information published by OFAC, serving as a reminder for businesses to conduct thorough due diligence and adhere to sanctions requirements.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to resolve its potential civil liability for apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs.
These violations include apparent breaches of sanctions related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism, underscoring the broad scope of compliance failures.

This settlement is part of a larger enforcement action, with FinCEN concurrently assessing a $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America for Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering (BSA/AML) deficiencies.

This enforcement action serves as a reminder for all businesses involved in international trade and logistics to implement robust compliance measures to prevent sanctions breaches.

The enforcement action serves as a stark warning about the personal consequences of failing to comply with U.S. sanctions regulations, emphasizing the need for individuals to understand and adhere to these rules.

articles.headline: EU and Indonesia Sign Comprehensive Economic Partnership and Investment Protection Agreements
body: The European Union and Indonesia have signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and an Investment Protection Agreement (IPA), marking a significant step in strengthening economic ties between the two regions. These agreements are expected to create new opportunities for businesses and deliver substantial economic benefits.

The CEPA and IPA are projected to boost economic growth, with the EU's GDP potentially increasing by €16 billion and Indonesia's by €27 billion within 15 years. EU exports to Indonesia are forecast to rise by almost 40%, particularly in machinery, motor vehicles, and other metals, while Indonesian exports to the EU are expected to increase by over 14%.

These agreements will remove import duties on 98.5% of tariff lines, simplify procedures for EU goods exports, and open new investment opportunities for EU companies in strategic Indonesian sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
